title: Arjuna's honest objection
hookLine: his legs give way, his mouth goes dry, the bow slips, and the greatest warrior alive makes his case against the war
carry: doubt gets heard in full before it's answered

lines: LEGS GIVE WAY, MOUTH GOES DRY.
cards: Think about the last time your body knew before you did. A phone call you didn't want to make, and your hands went cold. A room you didn't want to walk into, and your stomach turned.
Arjuna has just looked at his whole family lined up to fight him, and before he can make a single argument, his body makes it for him. His legs give way. His mouth dries up.
He's shaking. The hair on his arms stands up. His skin burns.
Gandiva, the well-known bow, starts slipping from his hand. He can't stand. Then the words come.

teach.b: Chapter one, verses twenty-eight to thirty-nine, is Arjuna's objection, and the Gita takes it seriously. Is it cowardice? Many readers hear conscience.
The heart of it, in Sanskrit: na cha shreyo 'nupashyami hatva svajanam ahave.

teach.h: I SEE NO GOOD IN KILLING MY KIN.
teach.b: I see no good in killing my own people in battle. Then further: na kankshe vijayam Krishna, na cha rajyam sukhani cha.
I don't want victory, Krishna, or a kingdom, or pleasures. What would a kingdom be for, he asks, if the people we wanted it for are lying dead on this field?
Even if they kill me, he says, I don't want to kill them, not for all three worlds, let alone this earth. Then his sharpest point.

teach.h: THEY CAN'T SEE. WE CAN. TURN BACK.
teach.b: Yes, the Kauravas are in the wrong; greed clouds their minds, and they can't see the evil of destroying a family. But we can, he says. Why shouldn't we, who see clearly, turn back?
And the Gita gives Arjuna twelve verses to make his case, fully, in his own words, before anyone answers. Krishna doesn't interrupt.
When he answers, in the next chapter, his first words are blunt: he calls this a weakness of the heart.
Commentators have argued ever since over whether it's conscience or confusion. Either way, it's built into Hinduism's best-loved book: the Gita is a dialogue, and doubt gets the first word.
The answer takes the rest of the book. A good teacher lets you say the whole thing.

how: Commentators on the Gita treat Arjuna's objection in 1.28–1.39 as a serious moral argument, and many readers see in it their own moments of doubt before a hard duty; the rest of the Gita is Krishna's answer to it.

games.q: what's inside the objection — tap the pairs.
p: Arjuna's bow, slipping from his hand

s: Krishna cuts Arjuna off halfway through his objection
the Gita gives him twelve verses to make his case in full before anyone answers.
Arjuna says he'd rather be killed than kill them
even if they kill me, he says, not for all three worlds.
Arjuna argues the Kauravas are in the right
he says they're blinded by greed, but that those who see clearly should turn back.

games.q: you're Arjuna. your family is lined up to fight you, your legs are shaking, and Krishna is waiting. what do you do?
o: grit your teeth and give the signal.
say everything you feel, all of it.
turn the chariot around and leave.
games.why: he makes his whole case: no victory, no kingdom is worth this. Krishna lets him finish before saying a word.

practice: Think of something in front of you that part of you really doesn't want to do, and first notice where your body tightens or goes cold. Then let the objection talk, fully, in its own words, the way Arjuna's does.
Don't answer, argue or shame it; just listen to the end.

wordCard.voice: Gandiva, Arjuna's well-known bow, slipping from his hand as his legs give way. Arjuna's case against the war: no victory, no kingdom, is worth the people he loves.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Gita 1.31: and I see no good. what follows: in killing my own people in battle.
